<meta>continues from previous page: ...white</meta> sulfur of nature is hardened, after a little heat, which pertains to silver, provided it is also informed with the form of silver, whereby it can become gold more easily than from other metals, unless it is deprived of its own heat or natural operation is taken from it. But if the power of a greater natural heat reaches this living silver <note>original: "argentum vivum"</note> before it is formed into its end, namely into the form of silver, so that it is reduced into a pure and red sulfur of nature, then gold is made from it more quickly than silver, and it remains in it perpetually, which is the end toward which nature strives by working.

Quicksilver, which we have just mentioned, is the mother of all metals, on account of its coldness and humidity: and if it is pure and separated from all superfluity, then no thickness can be mixed with it anymore, so that it might be reduced back into some imperfect metal. For Nature does not work backward, nor is there matter that looks to an impure form, such as imperfect metals are. But sulfur is the father of all metals, on account of its heat and dryness: let it be observed, according to this difference, that quicksilver is described in the following chapter.

## CHAPTER II.

**T**here is, therefore, in all metals a true <term>Mercury</term> <gloss>the alchemical principle of fluidity and spirit</gloss>, and a right sulfur, equally in imperfect as in perfect metals: it has only been made contaminated and impure in imperfect metals, which are deprived of only perfect maturation. And for the same causes they can be reduced to gold and silver, that is, so that the impurity with which they had been defiled is separated from the golden or silver nature that is in them, and the form of gold or silver is instilled into them. For they have been torn from nature for this reason, that they were taken out—dug up—from natural passages, mines, and veins of the earth: therefore they can no longer have any operation within themselves, as if they were still lying hidden under the earth; nevertheless, however, in as much as it is in them, they desire to be perfected.

<summary>This page continues the discussion of the generation of metals, defining quicksilver and sulfur as the universal "mother" and "father" of all metallic substances. It explains that imperfect metals are merely immature forms of gold and silver, which nature would eventually perfect if they remained undisturbed in the earth.</summary>
